title: Landing in Berlin & First Impressions
description: The journey begins! My first week settling into life and work in Berlin.

data.text: Arrival in Berlin 🇩🇪
I landed at Berlin Brandenburg Airport last Monday, excited but nervous. The city immediately struck me as both modern and historic—a mix of concrete minimalism and preserved history.
Settling In
My Airbnb is in Prenzlauer Berg — a quiet but lively neighborhood filled with bakeries, bikes, and young families. It’s perfect for easing into the Berlin rhythm.
First Day at the Startup 🚀
The team was super welcoming. I'm working as a frontend intern, primarily in React and TypeScript. Their codebase is actually cleaner than I expected, and I already got my first task merged!
“Berlin feels like a playground for creatives and builders.”
data.caption: me, after 4 cups of coffee

data.text: Overall, it’s been a fulfilling (and slightly chaotic) week. More updates coming soon!

title: Diving Into the Tech Stack
description: A deep dive into the technologies I’m using during my internship and how I adapted to the codebase.

data.text: Tech Stack Breakdown ⚙️
In my second week, I got a much clearer picture of the tech environment here. The team is building a SaaS analytics dashboard, and the stack is more modern than I expected.
Onboarding Challenges
The most challenging part wasn’t the stack — it was understanding the team’s conventions. Their folder structure and naming patterns are super opinionated, which took time to learn.
Another hurdle was figuring out how their internal component library worked. It’s built on top of Radix + Tailwind, and has its own theme context. It felt like a mini design system inside the app.
My First Real Contribution 🎉

After going through a couple of onboarding tasks, I picked up a ticket to refactor the user settings modal. I learned the hard way that making changes in a shared design system affects more things than you expect 😅.
“Naming things is still the hardest problem in computer science.”
data.caption: me, naming a function 'handleThing'

data.text: Despite the challenges, it’s rewarding to see my code running in production already. Next week I’ll be working on data visualizations!

title: Cultural Clashes and Cafe Code Sessions
description: Not everything about working abroad is about code. Here’s what surprised me about German work culture — and how I’ve found balance.

data.text: Work Culture Surprise 🇩🇪

One of the most unexpected challenges of this internship has been adjusting to the culture at work. Germans are punctual — painfully punctual. If a meeting starts at 09:00, you’d better be there at 08:59.
People are also super direct, which I initially took as cold. But I’m slowly learning that it’s not rude, it’s just... efficient. There’s no dancing around feedback, and honestly, that’s refreshing.
Cafe Coding ☕

After work, I’ve made it a habit to bring my laptop to a few local cafes. There’s one near Prenzlauer Berg where the Wi-Fi is strong and the espresso even stronger. There’s something magical about coding with soft jazz and espresso in the background.

items: Café Neue Liebe — Best vibe for deep focus

data.text: Languages Everywhere
At work, we speak English. On the street, it’s German. In the café, it’s a mix of French, Spanish, and Dutch. I’ve never been in such a linguistically diverse place — it’s chaotic and beautiful.
“You don’t need to be fluent in the language — you just need to be fluent in curiosity.”
data.caption: me, ordering coffee with 60% confidence

title: Landing in Bangkok: Chaos, Heat, and Smiles
description: First impressions of Southeast Asia, from street food stalls to tuk-tuks and temples. It’s overwhelming and exhilarating.

data.text: Touchdown in Thailand 🇹🇭

I arrived in Bangkok after a red-eye flight from Frankfurt. Jetlagged, sweaty, and completely unprepared for the humidity, I stepped out of Suvarnabhumi Airport straight into organized chaos — and I loved it instantly.
Sensory Overload

The air was thick with exhaust, grilled meat, incense, and what I think was durian. Tuk-tuks zoomed past me, their drivers yelling prices in broken English. Every street corner had a sizzling wok, a cart of fresh fruit, or someone selling knockoff sunglasses.

items: Pad Thai from a street vendor: $1.50 and divine.
Tried my first Thai iced tea — dangerously addictive.
Got scammed on a tuk-tuk ride within 2 hours of landing 😅

data.text: Wat Pho at Sunrise

Despite exhaustion, I forced myself to visit Wat Pho at 6:00am. The Reclining Buddha was massive and golden and peaceful. For a moment, the city noise faded, and it was just me and the monks chanting nearby.
“Travel isn’t always about escape. Sometimes it’s about being more present than ever.”
data.caption: me, sweating and barefoot in a temple

title: Train to Chiang Mai: The Long Ride North
description: An overnight train, chance encounters with travelers, and the slower rhythms of northern Thailand.

data.text: All Aboard the Night Train 🚆
After a whirlwind of Bangkok’s buzz, I booked a second-class sleeper train to Chiang Mai. 13 hours. No Wi-Fi. Thin mattress. Perfect setup to unwind and reflect.

My seat converted into a bunk bed. Curtains gave a hint of privacy. Across from me sat a German couple who were also backpacking. We exchanged itineraries and snacks (they had Haribo, I had sticky rice).
Stars Through the Window
Somewhere around midnight, I peeked out from behind the curtain and saw stars I hadn’t seen in years. It reminded me why I travel — to slow down and notice the world again.

items: Pro tip: Book lower bunks — they’re more stable and cooler.
The rhythmic clack of the tracks is better than any white noise app.

data.text: Morning Arrival
At 7:30 AM, we rolled into Chiang Mai. The city was misty and green. Compared to Bangkok, it felt like a calm exhale.
“Sometimes the best parts of a trip are the transitions.”
data.caption: – a sleepy me, disembarking with a backpack and a smile

title: Chiang Mai Temples & Street Food
description: Exploring sacred temples, chatting with monks, and tasting northern Thai cuisine that hits all the right notes.

data.text: Temple Mornings

Chiang Mai’s old city is surrounded by a square moat and ancient walls. I rented a bike and pedaled from temple to temple — Wat Chedi Luang, Wat Phra Singh, and smaller ones without names but with just as much beauty.

At Wat Suan Dok, I sat down for a ‘Monk Chat’. It’s exactly what it sounds like — young monks practicing English and sharing their way of life. One monk told me: ‘Peace is not in the temple. It’s in your breath.’
Afternoons of Spice and Smoke
In the afternoons, I wandered into food markets and let my nose do the guiding. I tried khao soi — a creamy, curry noodle soup that instantly became my favorite dish of the trip.

items: Sticky mango rice, warm and perfect
Thai iced tea in a plastic bag with a straw

data.text: “In Chiang Mai, food is a form of hospitality, not just business.”
data.caption: – a vendor at the North Gate night market

data.text: Golden Hours
I ended the day at a temple on a hill. Locals lit incense and rang bells. I didn’t understand the rituals, but I felt welcomed to witness them. The sky turned orange. The city slowed down. So did I.

title: Reflections in Cambodia
description: As my journey wrapped up in Cambodia, I found stillness among ancient ruins and new clarity on modern streets.

data.text: First Light at Angkor Wat

I woke up at 4:30am to catch the sunrise at Angkor Wat. The temple slowly revealed itself in the soft glow of dawn — still, proud, ancient. It was quiet except for the occasional camera shutter. I put mine down and just watched.

Later I wandered through Ta Prohm, the temple swallowed by trees. Roots twist through stone like nature reclaiming what was once hers. It reminded me of impermanence — of how time doesn’t take, it transforms.
From Ruins to Rooftops

Back in Phnom Penh, I walked the riverside at sunset. Monks with cellphones, tuk-tuks dodging potholes, street kids juggling fire for tips. Cambodia is layered — brutal history and resilient spirit living side by side.
“This is the new Cambodia. Not forgetting, just walking forward.”
data.caption: – a local guide named Dara

data.text: What I’m Taking Home

Three months. Three countries. A backpack, a journal, and a lot of noodles. But I leave with more than souvenirs — I’m bringing home presence, perspective, and peace. I used to think travel was about seeing the world. Now I think it’s about seeing yourself in it.
